newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees yuan rising on balance of payments.
newsitem.headline: China sees yuan rising on balance of payments.

text.p: The Chinese yuan is expected to rise further against the U.S. dollar in 1997 due to favourable balance of payments and the central bank's tight monetary policy, the China News Service said on Monday.

"Under the macro-environment created by the central bank's maintenance of an appropriately tight monetary policy, the trend of foreign exchange supply exceeding demand will become more significant next year," it quoted financial experts as saying.
"The renminbi will become stronger," it said.

In recent months the yuan has maintained upward momentum on the Shanghai-based interbank foreign exchange market, repeatedly hitting year-highs in July and August. It closed at 8.306 against the dollar on Monday, up from 8.3064 on last Friday.

The yuan's level would be mainly decided by China's balance of international payments, because its convertibility was still only partial, China News Service quoted the unidentified analysts as saying.
China has vowed to make the yuan convertible under the current account by the end of 1996.
A recent cut in interest rates would not have any significant impact on the balance of payments, the agency said.
The central bank cut deposit and lending rates by an average of 1.5 and 1.2 percentage points from August 23, but stressed the cut did not herald an easing of tight money policy.

China's foreign exchange reserves, swelled mainly by an inflow of foreign investments under the capital account, would remain stable after the rate cut because few foreign short-term investors had speculated on higher interest rates.
The rate cut could boost both exports and imports and would not affect the general balance of trade, the agency quoted the analysts as saying.
It would not lead to an outflow of foreign capital because of the yuan's limited convertibility, it said.
China's foreign exchange reserves hit a record $90.8 billion in July and are expected to climb to nearly $100 billion by the end of this year, officials have said.

A pressing task facing the central bank is to limit the further appreciation of the yuan without relaxing the tight money policy, the agency quoted Zhou Xiaochuan, head of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange Control as saying.
